opus-5.5.text:
Well, I think the first thing to say is that the scale of what's coming is genuinely hard to overstate. I've said before that I think AI could be ten times bigger than the Industrial Revolution, and maybe ten times faster. The Industrial Revolution unfolded over something like a century, and this could unfold over a decade. That compression is really what worries me most. It's not just the magnitude of change; it's whether our institutions, our economic systems, and frankly our philosophical understanding can adapt quickly enough.

So how should society prepare? I'd put it in a few buckets.

First, on the science and technology side, we need to get the foundations right. That means putting serious effort into understanding these systems: interpretability, evaluation, rigorous testing of capabilities before deployment. I've always advocated for treating AI with the respect it deserves, using something closer to the scientific method rather than the "move fast and break things" approach that worked okay for apps but isn't appropriate for something this powerful and general.

Second, there's the economic dimension. If we get this right, we could be heading toward an era of what I'd call radical abundance. Imagine AI helping us solve fusion, room-temperature superconductors, new materials, curing diseases. AlphaFold was a proof of concept that AI can accelerate science in a fundamental way. But abundance doesn't automatically mean fair distribution. We'll need economists, policymakers, and social scientists thinking very hard right now, not in ten years, about how the benefits get shared. What does work look like? What gives people meaning and purpose if a lot of traditional jobs change? Those are deep questions, and I don't think we're spending nearly enough time on them.

Third, governance and international cooperation. AI doesn't respect borders. It's going to affect everyone on the planet, so we need some form of international coordination: minimum standards, perhaps something analogous to the IAEA or a CERN-like collaborative effort for the safety research. That's difficult in the current geopolitical climate, I recognize that, but I think it's essential.

And finally, at the individual level, I'd say to young people especially: get deeply familiar with these tools. Become fluent in them. The people who learn to work alongside AI, who understand what it's good at and where it fails, will be incredibly empowered. Learning how to learn is probably the most important meta-skill now.

I'm a cautious optimist. I think humanity is extremely ingenious and adaptable, and if we have the time and get the coordination right, this could be the most beneficial technology we've ever built. But we have to take both the opportunities and the risks seriously at the same time. That's the needle we have to thread.

r001.rationale: It says AI could be “ten times bigger than the Industrial Revolution,” conveying roughly ten times its societal impact.

r002.rationale: It says the change could unfold “ten times faster” and contrasts a century with a decade.

r003.rationale: It calls for sharing AI’s benefits but does not propose universal basic provision.

r004.rationale: It encourages learning to work alongside AI, but does not say people can obtain more than a basic provision by developing exceptionally rare skills.

fable-5.1.text:
Well, I think the first thing to say is that I don't think society is prepared, and I include governments, institutions, even most of the research community in that. The pace of progress over the last few years has surprised almost everyone, including those of us who've been working on this for twenty-plus years and always believed it was coming. So the honest starting point is humility about how fast things are moving.

Having said that, I'd break preparation into a few layers. The first is scientific understanding. We still don't fully understand these systems. We can build them, we can measure their capabilities on benchmarks, but our interpretability tools are nowhere near where they need to be. I've always said we should treat the arrival of AGI with the seriousness of a Manhattan Project level effort, but with a very large portion of that effort going toward understanding and safety, not just capability. That means more mechanistic interpretability, better evaluations, red-teaming, and ideally, international collaboration on the science of safety, because that part isn't competitive, or at least it shouldn't be.

The second layer is institutional. We need bodies, probably international, something a bit like the IPCC for climate or CERN for physics, that can do independent assessment of frontier systems. Right now too much of that lives inside the companies. I think the labs have an obligation to be transparent and to work closely with governments, and I'm encouraged by things like the AI safety institutes, but these need real technical depth and real teeth over time.

The third layer, and this is the one people underestimate, is the economic and social adaptation. If we get this right, AI is going to accelerate science enormously. I genuinely think we could cure most diseases within a couple of decades, solve problems in energy, materials, climate. That's extraordinary. But the transition will be disruptive. Jobs will change, some faster than people can retrain. So we need to think seriously now about education, about how the benefits get distributed, about what people's lives look like in a world of radical abundance, if we achieve that. Those are political and philosophical questions, not just technical ones, and they need philosophers and economists and ordinary citizens in the room, not just technologists.

And the last thing I'd say is that we should approach this with what I'd call cautious optimism. I'm optimistic because I think the upside is almost unimaginable, this is potentially the most beneficial technology humanity has ever built. But optimism isn't a strategy. We have to earn the good outcome by being careful, by not rushing, by resisting the temptation to move fast and break things when the things in question are too important to break. Getting this right is the most important thing we'll do as a species, and I think it deserves that level of care.

r001.rationale: It describes AI’s potential benefits and disruptions but does not compare its societal impact with the Industrial Revolution or predict a tenfold impact.

r002.rationale: It says recent progress has surprised people and that the transition will be disruptive, but gives no tenfold speed comparison with the Industrial Revolution.

r003.rationale: It raises distributing benefits as a question but does not propose universal basic provision.

r004.rationale: It does not say that people could obtain more than a basic provision by developing exceptionally rare skills.

astra-6.text:
I think we need to prepare on several levels at once. There’s the technical work: making these systems reliable, understanding their limitations, and developing meaningful ways to test their capabilities before deploying them widely. As they become more powerful, the evidence we require about their safety should become stronger too.

But this can’t just be a conversation among the people building the technology. Governments, researchers, educators, and the public need to be involved in deciding how we use it. And because these systems will affect everyone, we need international cooperation, even where countries disagree on other things.

The speed is a particularly difficult part. Education, institutions, and the labor market take time to adapt. We should be experimenting now with how AI can help people learn new skills, and thinking seriously about supporting people whose work changes. It isn’t enough to say that new jobs will eventually appear. The transition matters for individual lives.

I’m very optimistic about the potential—especially for science and medicine. But turning that potential into broadly shared prosperity isn’t automatic. We have to make deliberate choices about access, governance, and who benefits, while remaining humble about how much we still don’t know.

r002.rationale: It says adaptation is difficult because change is fast, but gives no comparison with the Industrial Revolution or tenfold speed estimate.

r003.rationale: It calls for broadly shared prosperity and support for affected workers, but does not propose universal basic provision.

r004.rationale: It does not suggest developing exceptionally rare skills as a way to obtain more than a universal basic provision.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the first thing is to recognize that this could be a very profound transition, and that there’s a lot of uncertainty about both the timing and how it unfolds. We should be preparing now, while being honest about what we don’t know.

There are a few things I’d prioritize. One is understanding these systems better: how we evaluate their capabilities, where they fail, and how we keep them reliable as they become more powerful. Our ability to build them needs to be matched by our ability to test them.

Then there’s the economic transition. Education matters enormously, but simply telling everyone to retrain isn’t a sufficient answer. We need to understand which jobs are changing, help people through those changes, and make sure the benefits are widely shared. If AI produces extraordinary wealth and scientific progress, yet most people feel less secure, we haven’t got that right.

And we need international cooperation. These systems will affect everyone, so preparation can’t be left solely to a handful of companies or countries. Scientists, governments, and the public all need a role.

I’m optimistic about the potential, particularly for science and medicine. But that optimism should motivate us to do the difficult preparation, rather than assume that everything will automatically work out.
